blueprint.ending_payoff: Return to the quiet first night of the opening, now understood: the night when 'nothing happened' was the moment every clock the Moon kept (the tide's, the reef's, the owl's, the day's, the axis') began to lose its beat, each on its own timescale, from hours to a million years. The Moon was never mainly a lamp; it was Earth's metronome, and how far the slowest of those clocks would drift is still an open question.

beats.experience: Intrigued and a little disarmed: the viewer expects an apocalypse and gets a quiet, darker night, with the promise that the real story is slower and stranger.
beats.visual_intent: A painted coast under a moonless sky, the Milky Way brighter than usual; then a drawn Earth-Moon diagram where the Moon is only a dashed empty outline: absence shown, not an explosion.

hedges.R1: This can't happen, so let's simply suppose it: tonight the Moon is gone, its light and its pull, and nothing else in the sky changes.

beats.experience: Surprise that the sea keeps moving, and a first 'so that's whose tide it is'.
beats.visual_intent: A harbour wall with old painted tide marks and a much narrower band where the water now rises and falls; a drawn diagram of the Moon's and the Sun's tidal pulls side by side, the Sun's arrow a little under half as long.

hedges.R2: Work it through: the Sun still pulls on the oceans with a little less than half the Moon's force, so the tide doesn't vanish; it shrinks to the Sun's share.

beats.experience: The pleasure of a pattern noticed: the tide was always a Moon clock, and now it stops drifting.
beats.visual_intent: A drawn tide chart: today's waves swelling and shrinking over two weeks, then an even row of identical waves; above each high tide a small clock face whose hands creep forward day by day, then stay on the same hour.

hedges.R3: Which means two things follow: no more spring or neap tides, and high water at about the same hour every day.

beats.experience: A jolt: the thought experiment has, in a small way, already been run, and a living thing lost its timing.
beats.visual_intent: A night reef a few nights after a full Moon, corals releasing bundles that rise like slow snow; then a laboratory tank beside a drawn monthly calendar, its release dots scattered across the month instead of clustered in one week.
beats.key_moment: the coral experiment: the Moon's rhythm taken away, the larvae out of step

significance.matters_because: Until here every consequence was reasoned; this is the first one observed. One coral, denied the Moon's changing light, lost the timing it shares with its reef, so the viewer sees that the Moon's clock is something living things actually read, not a poetic idea.
significance.reward: the jolt of finding that the experiment has already been done, on one species

depends_on.what: the rule of the game: the Moon's light and pull are gone, nothing else changes
the Moon as a clock: the tide's rhythm and how it would stop drifting

beats.experience: An honest open question: concern without doom.
beats.visual_intent: A northern rocky shore at low water, tiny midges over wet stone, white water churning; a drawn split panel, one half showing the cues their clocks are known to use, the other half left blank for what nobody knows.

hedges.R5: Would they find another clock? Some already have a second cue, but how these animals keep lunar time is still poorly understood, so honestly, nobody knows.

beats.experience: Seeing the night as information, and a quiet strangeness: the month stops at new Moon for good.
beats.visual_intent: Painted night scenes in turn: an eagle owl calling from a high perch under a bright Moon, then the same perch in darkness; a coyote howling under a moonless sky; a flock leaving a dark coast; a drawn strip of Moon phases that runs out at new Moon and stays dark.

hedges.R6: So every night becomes a new-moon night, and the animals that already behave differently in the dark would live in that half of their month for good.

beats.experience: A widening of scale: the day itself turns out to be one of the Moon's clocks.
beats.visual_intent: A drawn Earth seen from above the pole, its two tidal bulges dragged slightly ahead and acting as a brake on the spin; below, a long timeline of the day's length rising from left to right, its slope flattening where the Moon's share of the brake is taken away.

hedges.R7: And because the Moon raises the larger share of those tides, taking it away leaves only the Sun's weaker tide as a brake: the day would still lengthen, just more slowly.

beats.experience: Awe at the slowest, largest consequence: the planet's axis, steady through all of human history, begins to wander.
beats.visual_intent: A painted globe with its axis at 23 degrees and a thin band showing how little it moves now; then the band opens into a fan from 15 to 32 degrees along a million-year timeline, with a strip of seasons beneath growing milder and harsher as the fan swings.

significance.matters_because: The tilt is what makes the seasons, and the Moon is what has kept it steady. Losing the Moon would let the seasons themselves drift over a million years: the one consequence that reaches the climate of the whole planet.
significance.reward: awe at the scale, and the satisfaction of seeing the Moon's least visible job
significance.self_contained: what the tilt is, why it makes the seasons and how the Moon steadies it are all drawn inside this beat; it needs only the premise the viewer has held since the start

hedges.R8: In one calculation that took the Moon away from today's Earth, the tilt wandered between 15 and 32 degrees within a million years.

beats.experience: Honesty as its own reward: the viewer learns where the knowledge stops, and why a confident answer would overreach.
beats.visual_intent: Two drawn panels side by side: a globe with a very wide fan of axis positions next to a small sketch of a faster-spinning early Earth (the conditions of the large result), and the same globe drifting slowly along a much longer timeline.

hedges.R9: How far it would go in the long run, the scientists who modelled it still disagree: one classic study says almost anywhere, given enough time; later work says it would happen far more slowly.

beats.experience: Recognition and quiet satisfaction: the opening night now means something new.
beats.visual_intent: The opening coast again under the moonless sky, now with faint drawn overlays of every clock the film met (the tide line, the reef calendar, the owl's perch, the day's timeline, the axis fan), each fading at its own pace.

significance.matters_because: It answers the opening question with a different picture of the Moon: not the night's lamp but the keeper of time for the sea, for living things and for the planet's axis. The quiet first night the viewer started with turns out to be the start of every change the film followed.
significance.reward: the click of the ending recasting the opening

depends_on.what: the quiet first night and the rule of the game
living things reading the Moon's calendar

hedges.R10: Put together, that is what losing the Moon would really mean: not one night of disaster, but every clock it keeps slowly losing its beat.
